messages.text: Will a power spike fry the whole miner?

Great question — and it's one of the real design wins on the Rev 6.1.

**The onboard F1 fuse takes the hit, not your miner.**

- There's a small automotive-style blade fuse (**F1**) mounted right on the board, next to the yellow XT30 power input.
- If a spike hits, **F1 blows first** — sacrificing a cheap fuse to protect everything behind it.
- Cheaper miners skip this entirely, so a spike goes straight into the electronics and kills the whole unit.

**Here it costs you a fuse, not a miner.**

The X.30 connector itself also helps — rated at **15 A**, it replaced the old Rev 5 barrel jack (only 8 A) that was the classic failure point at high load. Paired with the thicker PCB copper, the whole power path is built to take punishment.
What stops it from overheating or dying?

Several layers working together on the Rev 6.1:

**1. Spring-mounted heatsink**
Springs press the sink evenly across all 4× BM1370 dies — no single "hot corner" chip cooking faster than the rest.

**2. Custom BSB airflow shroud**
A black 3D-printed duct routes fan air directly onto the **voltage regulators (VRMs)** — the part that quietly kills most small miners first. Most boards leave VRMs bare. Here they get dedicated airflow.

**3. VRM temps at full load: ~54 °C**
That's the usual first-to-fail part, kept well in check. ASIC core sits around **~57 °C** at full 6 TH/s / 800 MHz.

**4. Oversized PSU loafing at ~30% load**
The included **350 W MEANWELL** feeds a ~100 W miner — running cool and well within its limits 24/7, rather than a stressed cheap brick that degrades fast.

**5. Onboard F1 fuse**
As above — power spikes blow the fuse, not the board.

**Result:** ~40–45 dB, desk-friendly, designed to run continuously without the classic small-miner failure modes. Quiet because it doesn't *need* to scream to stay cool.
